title: On the Convergence Direction of Gradient Descent
claim: Gradient descent converges either along a fixed direction under small step sizes or oscillates along an alternating line under large step sizes.
layout: 2x2 grid of contour plots; rows are functions, columns are step sizes
description: Four contour-plot panels in a 2x2 grid, each with its own viridis-style Loss Value colorbar on the right. Each panel shows a red GD trajectory starting at a green star (initial point), with a legend in the upper right. Black arrows mark the two coordinate axes at the origin or limit point. The top row uses a quadratic function and the bottom row uses a function with extra cubic terms. In the left column, with a small learning rate, the red path curves smoothly into the minimum along the x-axis. In the right column, with a large learning rate, the path zigzags with shrinking amplitude and alternates along the y-axis. The eye goes first to the red trajectories against the purple-to-yellow contours.
caption: GD trajectories for f(x, y) = x2/2 + 2y2 with η = 0.1 (upper left, the convergence direction exists as x-axis) and η = 0.42 (upper right, the convergence direction alternates along yaxis), and for f(x, y) = x2/2 + 2y2 + xy2 + y3 with η = 0.1 (lower left, the convergence direction exists as x-axis) and η = 0.42 (lower right, the convergence direction alternates along y-axis).
abstract: Gradient descent (GD) is a fundamental optimization method in deep learning, yet its asymptotic directional properties remain less understood. In this paper, we prove that if GD converges, its trajectory either aligns toward a fixed direction or oscillates along a specific line. The fixed-direction convergence occurs under small learning rates, while the oscillatory convergence behavior emerges for large learning rates. This result offers a new lens for understanding long-term GD dynamics. Experimentally, we find that this directional convergence behavior also appears in stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and Adam. Furthermore, we discuss how these theoretical findings regarding oscillatory convergence might offer a perspective on the sharpness dynamics observed in the Edge of Stability (EoS) regime. Our work provides both theoretical clarity and practical insight into the behavior of dynamics for multiple optimization methods.
